blocks.text: When two waves of the same wavelength overlap at a point, the principle of superposition explains what we observe. Two coherent waves meeting in a region reinforce each other at some points and cancel at others, forming a pattern called interference. Consider two loudspeakers producing sounds of the same frequency and wavelength, connected to the same source so that they emit waves in phase. At some points the two waves arrive in phase (in step) with equal amplitude; the resultant has twice the amplitude of a single wave and we hear a louder sound. At other points they arrive half a cycle out of step and cancel, and we hear a quieter sound (Fig 15.3).

items: The waves must be of the same type: sound waves can interfere only with other sound waves.
The waves must be coherent, with a constant phase difference.
The waves must be moving in the same, or almost the same, direction.

blocks.text: Waves of different amplitudes can still interfere, but the contrast between bright and dark (or loud and quiet) regions is reduced.

blocks.alt: Three graphs of displacement (in units of 10^-4 m, from -4 to 4) against time. (a) Blue and green waves of amplitude 2 lie on top of each other; the pink resultant has amplitude 4. (b) Blue and green waves of amplitude 2 are half a cycle apart; the resultant is a flat line along the time axis. (c) A blue wave of amplitude 1 and a green wave of amplitude 2 in phase give a pink resultant of amplitude 3.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.3: Adding waves by the principle of superposition. Blue and green waves of the same amplitude may give (a) constructive or (b) destructive interference; (c) waves of different amplitudes can also interfere constructively (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.3).

blocks.text: We are surrounded by many waves, such as visible light, infrared, radio waves and sound, yet we do not see interference patterns all the time. We can see interference in everyday life, for example haloes of light around street lamps or the Moon on a foggy night, or light and dark bands when looking at a bright light through fabric, but measurable effects usually need specially arranged conditions. If the two loudspeakers were connected to different signal generators with slightly different frequencies, the waves might start in phase but would soon go out of phase (Fig 15.4); we would hear loud, then soft, then loud again, and the pattern would keep shifting around the room.

blocks.alt: Displacement against time for a pink wave and a blue wave of slightly different wavelengths. Both start at 0; their first crests coincide (labelled in phase). They drift apart until, at a dashed vertical line labelled out of phase, a crest of the blue wave meets a trough of the pink wave.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.4: Waves of slightly different wavelengths and therefore waves move in and out of phase with one another (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.4).

blocks.title: Coherent sources
blocks.text: Coherent sources emit waves with a constant phase difference. Two waves can keep a constant phase difference only if their frequencies are the same and stay constant. Connecting both loudspeakers to the same signal generator makes them coherent sources.

Two lasers of the same frequency would not do: light from a laser is made of many separate bursts, and we cannot guarantee that the bursts from two lasers stay in phase. The problem is solved by using a single laser and dividing its light with two slits (Fig 15.5). The slits act as two coherent sources with a constant phase difference. If they were not coherent, the pattern would change far too fast for our eyes, and we would see only a uniform band of light without definite bright and dark regions.

blocks.alt: Three red wave trains. The top one shows a sudden change of phase, marked by an arrow. A blue slide with a double slit stands across the middle train. A vertical line through all three trains shows that the change of phase happens at the same place in each.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.5: Waves must be coherent if they are to produce a clear interference pattern (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.5).
